SpaceX plans to construct, own and operate a gas-fired power plant and super-compute facility at its company town in Starbase, Texas, according to a notice of a public hearing on the city’s website.
The estimated investment for the initial phase of the project is $24 billion. The city commissioner will consider the approval of a tax abatement and development agreement at a Dec. 9 meeting.
The proposal is the latest sign that CEO Elon Musk is seeking to vertically integrate SpaceX’s value chain for natural gas, the primary power-plant fuel that data center developers are using to get the facilities up and running. SpaceX is also looking to fuel some of its rocket launches with a super-chilled and purified form of the gas.
In September, SpaceX proposed building its own pipeline in Florida to transport gas to its Starship rockets in Cape Canaveral. The company has also been hiring gas traders in Starbase and Cape Canaveral to support its growing fuel and power needs, rather than relying on external logistics companies.
Starbase, incorporated in 2025, is home to several hundred SpaceX employees and their families. The proposed project is located within the corporate limits of Starbase on a 444-acre tract east of the city of Brownsville, according to the public notice.
Surging power needs from data centers and new factories have driven demand for gas plants, and Musk has long been a proponent for vertical integration. SpaceX also plans to build its own gas-fired power plant to support the massive semiconductor manufacturing facility it’s developing in Grimes County, outside of Houston, with Tesla Inc.
Musk’s prospects for getting a “super-compute facility” and associated gas infrastructure online could face headwinds from Texas’ incoming Democratic governor Gina Hinojosa, who ran in part on a promise to tame new data center construction. Rising power prices and concerns around the environmental impact of the facilities have triggered protests around the country, including ones against SpaceXSI’s data center complex in Memphis.

U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth listens to question during a news conference at the Pentagon on March 2, 2026 in Arlington, Virginia. (Photo by Alex Wong/Getty Images)
U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth struck a defiant tone Tuesday as he faces potential impeachment by the U.S. House of Representatives this week, casting the effort as an attack on American service members.
Hegseth during a rare news conference at the Pentagon called the impeachment effort a “farce” and flatly rejected the notion that he had committed impeachable offenses as the top civilian leader of the military. He likened himself to President Donald Trump, who was twice impeached during his first term.
“Let’s be clear about what this resolution actually does. It tells our enemies — Iran, the cartels, every adversary watching — that the United States will actually punish its own warriors and its own civilian leadership for successfully executing lawful military operations,” Hegseth said.
The House, led by Republicans during the lame-duck session following the Nov. 3 election, is set to vote on impeaching Hegseth as soon as Wednesday, with a procedural vote expected later Tuesday.
Massie impeachment articles
Rep. Thomas Massie, an outgoing Kentucky Republican, introduced articles of impeachment Monday alleging the defense secretary waged unlawful war against Iran, ordered extrajudicial killings and ignored laws intended to minimize civilian casualties, among other charges.
Impeachment would represent an extraordinary rebuke of one of the most divisive members of Trump’s Cabinet. Democrats, as well as some Republicans, are expected to support the effort, raising the possibility the articles will pass and trigger a trial in the Senate, though the outcome is unclear there.
Hegseth, a 46-year-old former Fox News personality who narrowly won Senate confirmation last year, has sought to project a swashbuckling, masculine image as the military’s top civilian leader. He has rebranded the Department of Defense as the “Department of War,” purged numerous high-ranking officers and tried to kick critical media outlets out of the Pentagon.
On Tuesday, Hegseth called Massie a “disgruntled and defeated congressman” who is attempting a “political spectacle” driven by ego and resentment. Massie, who has often clashed with Trump, lost his primary in May to a Trump-backed challenger.
“It’s a farce and it’s a stunt and everybody knows it,” Hegseth said.
Drug boats
Massie told reporters on Monday that Hegseth’s conduct of the military has endangered Americans.
As an example, he pointed to a second strike conducted on survivors of a suspected drug boat in the Caribbean that had already been hit, suggesting it will encourage enemies of the U.S. to act similarly in the future. Hegseth has denied ordering the strike, but said he supported it.
Massie dismissed Hegseth’s attacks on him, adding that he was “being polite” by using the impeachment process, which would only remove Hegseth from office but not subject him to criminal charges.
“Well, he’s right about one thing, I’m a defeated congressman. I’m not disgruntled,” Massie said.

Missouri among 3 states declining hardship exceptions to Medicaid work requirements
The state says existing exemptions will protect people facing medical emergencies, but experts warn some patients could fall through the cracks
While the Missouri Department of Social Services initially signaled it would adopt optional hardship exceptions for hospitalizations, medical travel and residence in disaster areas, it indicated last month that it believes it can accommodate many people in those categories through other provisions in federal law (Thomas Barwick/Getty Images).
After a Tyson Foods meatpacking plant closed in Nebraska in January, eliminating about 3,000 jobs, the state secured a temporary reprieve from new Medicaid work requirements for residents of the surrounding county.
Nebraska began enforcing work requirements in May, requiring most adults ages 19 to 64 covered through Medicaid expansion to work, attend school or volunteer 80 hours a month to get or maintain health coverage. A month later, the state sought federal approval to exempt residents of Dawson County, where unemployment had surged following the plant’s closure.
Missouri is one of just three states that have decided not to offer similar protections when the federal requirements take effect nationwide Jan. 1.
The Missouri Department of Social Services said last month that it will not adopt optional short-term hardship exceptions allowed in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act — including one that temporarily suspends work requirements in counties with unemployment rates at or above 8%, or 1.5 times the national average.
Six of the eight states bordering Missouri — Nebraska, Oklahoma, Arkansas, Tennessee, Kentucky and Illinois — plan to offer short-term hardship exceptions.
Kansas is not subject to the new requirements because it has not expanded Medicaid or adopted comparable coverage through a federal waiver.
Iowa and Indiana are the other two states declining all four exceptions.
In addition to areas with high unemployment, the short-term hardship exceptions cover extended travel for medical treatment for oneself or a dependent, areas with a federally declared emergency or disaster an inpatient or acute outpatient care in a hospital, nursing facility or intermediate care facility for people with intellectual disabilities.
States can adopt either all or none of the short-term exceptions, but the county-level exceptions for unemployment or disasters only go into effect after additional state action.
In an email to The Independent in October, Baylee Watts, media director for the department, said Missouri plans to accommodate “situations such as acute medical events and travel for specialized medical care” through mandatory exemptions for “medical frailty” and caregivers.
Federal law requires states to exempt people who are medically frail, including those who are blind or disabled, have substance use disorders, disabling mental disorders, serious or complex medical conditions, or physical, intellectual or developmental disabilities that significantly impair daily activities.

Costs for goods and services rose more than expected in October, providing fresh warning signs for the Federal Reserve in its fight to lower inflation.
The consumer price index, a broad gauge of costs across the U.S. economy, increased a seasonally adjusted 0.4% for the month, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Tuesday. Economists surveyed by Dow Jones had been looking for a 0.3% increase.
Stripping out volatile food and energy, so-called core CPI increased 0.3% against the forecast for a 0.2% gain.
The headline CPI had increased 0.6% in September while core was up 0.3%.
The report comes at a critical juncture for the Federal Reserve as it considers its next interest-rate move. Speaking Tuesday morning in London ahead of the CPI release, Fed Governor Christopher Waller said a hot inflation report could push him toward advocating for a half-point increase in December, and specifically said such a hike should be on the table if core CPI was "around 0.3."
Hours later, that's exactly what happened.
Traders are now fully pricing in a quarter percentage-point increase when the Fed next meets Dec. 8-9, and put odds of a half-point hike at 13.6%, after being around zero prior to the inflation report, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool.
Stocks fell following the release, while Treasury yields jumped.
"This was the report the market could least afford to see," said Karen Manna, fixed income investment strategist at Federated Hermes. "A hotter inflation print raises fresh questions about whether the Fed has done enough to contain price pressures and reinforces the risk that interest rates need to move higher and stay there for longer."
The BLS did not estimate a yearly rate in its October inflation report. The government shutdown last year prevented the bureau from collecting sufficient data in October 2025, so there is no comparable figure to use. However, the report did include annual figures for some individual items where it was able to collect data.
Though gasoline prices have been falling in recent weeks, the energy index rose 0.7% and the gasoline index was up 1%. The natural gas index, though, was off 0.8%.
Food costs accelerated 0.5%, pushed higher by increases of 1% for snacks, 0.9% for beef and 0.5% for meats, poultry, fish and eggs. Transportation services jumped 0.8%. New vehicle prices increased 0.2% but used cars and trucks fell 1.2%.
Shelter costs were higher by 0.3%, which the BLS said accounted for more than 30% of the headline increase.
Apparel, a tariff-sensitive sector, rose just 0.1%. Medical care commodities prices increased 0.5%. Airline fares accelerated 0.4%.
At the Fed's October meeting, central bank officials voted 10-2 to keep their benchmark rate in a range between 3.75%-4% while awaiting incoming data.
Markets already had been expecting the Fed to hike its benchmark borrowing rate next month, but the inflation data may have sealed the deal.
Despite the moderating gas prices recently, Fed officials have expressed concern that the impacts from the Iran war and President Donald Trump's tariffs are becoming embedded in the economy. Inflation has been running above the Fed's 2% target for some 5½ years.

Americans stomached higher grocery prices ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday. October's headline inflation data came in hotter than expected, driven by some key fixings for the holiday meal.
The Consumer Price Index rose 0.4% in October from the previous month, higher than the 0.3% economists were expecting but below September's 0.6% gain. Grocery prices increased 0.4% month over month, after remaining relatively flat over the past two months. The report does not include annual price changes because of the government shutdown in October 2025.
The monthly increases in food prices are likely due to seasonal demand, higher sugar prices, and higher energy costs, with gas and diesel prices remaining persistently high.
But there's some good news: Wells Fargo found that a Thanksgiving meal this year will actually cost Americans slightly less than it did last year. According to Wells Fargo's analysis, published on Monday ahead of the CPI report, the Thanksgiving food basket for a table of 10 will cost $78.93 this year, down 0.4% from a year ago.
The biggest price pressure comes from spending on wine and beer. Factoring in beverages, an overall Thanksgiving meal will run $127.54, or $12.75 per person.
Read more: October inflation breakdown includes cheaper gas, bigger grocery bills
How prices of key Thanksgiving items shifted last month
On a monthly basis, the star of the Thanksgiving table grew more expensive in October. The latest inflation data showed that prices for turkey and other uncooked poultry increased by 1.9% month over month.
If you're looking to swap turkey for another protein, ham prices are down, but prices for uncooked ground beef and beef steaks remain higher. Compared with the prior month, ground beef prices rose 1.2% as US cattle inventory remains at record lows.
Prices for fresh vegetables rose 2.2%, driven higher by lettuce, which is up 7.9% as higher diesel costs take a toll on American farmers. The Missouri Supreme Court on Tuesday rejected a challenge to the state’s stadium subsidy law, ruling that two Republican lawmakers and a conservative activist lacked the legal standing to contest its constitutionality.
In a 5-2 decision, the court upheld a Cole County judge’s dismissal of a lawsuit filed by state Sen. Mike Moon, an Ash Grove Republican, state Rep. Bryant Wolfin, a Ste. Genevieve Republican, and conservative activist Ron Calzone.
The ruling leaves the law intact without addressing the plaintiffs’ allegations that it violates several provisions of the Missouri Constitution.
Gov. Mike Kehoe signed the legislation in June 2025 after calling lawmakers into special session amid a bidding war with Kansas over the Kansas City Chiefs and Royals.
The law authorized state aid worth up to half the cost of qualifying stadium projects, along with tax incentives and property tax relief. The Chiefs have since announced plans to move to Kansas, while the Royals are pursuing a new ballpark near downtown Kansas City that could receive substantial state subsidies.
The lawsuit alleged the legislation violated constitutional restrictions requiring bills to contain a single subject, have a clear title and not stray from their original purpose. It also challenged the use of public money to benefit private businesses.
But the Supreme Court never reached those questions.
Writing for the majority, Judge Robin Ransom concluded the plaintiffs failed to demonstrate the direct expenditure of taxpayer money necessary to establish standing.
The challengers pointed to a fiscal analysis estimating the Missouri Department of Revenue would spend $10,000 creating a tax form and potentially $175,000 on computer programming to implement portions of the law.
Ransom rejected that argument, finding the estimates were speculative rather than evidence of actual spending.
“Projections are not equivalent to the requirement that a sum be paid out,” she wrote.
The majority also rejected the argument that the stadium subsidies themselves established standing. Any state expenditure, Ransom wrote, would require several additional steps, including an application, government approval and legislative appropriation.
The court likewise reaffirmed a 2011 precedent holding that tax credits generally do not constitute direct government expenditures for purposes of taxpayer standing.

Your race bib can tell organizers a lot more than how quickly you finished. At Spain's 61st edition of Behobia–San Sebastián, it also helped them figure out whether you started when you were supposed to. As it turns out, getting a little too eager at the starting line can be enough to cost you an official result.
Organizers confirmed that 853 participants were disqualified from the November 8 event, a popular 20K race that attracted 27,172 runners this year. According to Spanish outlets Mundo Deportivo and 3Cat, starting in an earlier wave than assigned was a major reason behind the unusually high number.
The race sorts participants into groups based on their previous performances, with staggered start times designed to help manage the crowds. Runners can move back to a later wave if they wish, but jumping ahead to an earlier one is grounds for disqualification. It's a rule that should sound familiar to anyone who's run a race with NYRR, as they follow the same policy and warn that moving into a faster wave or corral can cost runners their results.
With thousands of people lining up, slipping into an earlier group can go unnoticed, but timing chips attached to race bibs allow organizers to track when participants cross the starting line and other checkpoints along the course.
Other violations, including using another runner's bib without an authorized transfer, are against the rules and can also result in disqualification. However, organizers haven't provided explanations for every case, making it unclear how many involved starting-wave violations.
According to figures released by organizers, 29,301 people registered for the event, and 26,947 crossed the 12.4-mile course’s finish line in San Sebastián. Of those who completed the race, a little more than 3 percent were disqualified.
While it sounds like a lot, 853 is actually an improvement compared to previous years. In 2023, a whopping 1,327 runners were disqualified, followed by 958 in 2024 and 918 last year. So the numbers are heading in the right direction, although there's clearly still some confusion—or disregard—when it comes to following the pre-start rules.

Many experienced runners often assume that the run/walk method is only suitable for beginners. There’s no way it could help you reach your goals or allow you to run faster paces, right? In reality, it could be the missing piece of your training and racing plan.
Andrea Dell, an RRCA-certified run coach based in Charlotte, North Carolina, believes run/walk has a place in your training—no matter your fitness level or your goals. In fact, she includes some form of the run/walk method in all her runners’ training, because it’s a tried-and-true strategy for tackling longer distances, recovering more efficiently, and even dropping minutes from your marathon time.
So whether you’re a couch-to-5K runner, a first-time marathoner, or a seasoned athlete, Dell lays out all the ways run/walk can improve your training and how to make the most of the method.
What Run/Walk Can Look Like for Every Runner
If you’re a first-time runner or someone following a couch-to-5K training plan, your run/walk intervals might look like 30 seconds of running followed by a 60-second walk interval.
If you’re a first-time marathoner or a more advanced runner, however, you might run for four minutes followed by 30-second walks. More advanced runners or those going for long distances might also use run/walk intervals during workouts such as Yasso 800s. To do it, run 800 meters at the prescribed pace, but instead of jogging between efforts, walk briskly to recover. This walk interval should be double the amount of time of the hard effort, Dell says.
While run/walk intervals can serve as a speed workout hack to help you get faster and pace more evenly (more on that below), they can improve your running in other ways, too. For example, try 90-second run intervals and 30-second walks for extra recovery on an easy run the day after a long run. This reduces the overall stress of the effort, but still gets your legs turning over so you can move through any soreness without stiffening up, Dell explains.
You can also use run/walk intervals during your weekend long runs to help you conquer the distance.
The Benefits of Run/Walk Intervals for Every Level of Runner
Run Farther
If you want to run farther distances, “run/walk keeps your heart rate low for long enough that you can maintain pace for a lot longer than you would expect,” says Dell. This makes it a lot more manageable to tackle a half or full marathon for the first time (or if you’re racing the distance again after a long time away).

Management said brand advertising declined mainly because of lower spending by consumer packaged goods companies, driven by macro pressures in the U.S. and the Middle East. Management also said direct response ads keep growing as a share of Snap’s business, which it expects to continue in the short term, and that improvements in its brand products and sales approach should kick in as Snap moves into 2027. Both are management’s expectations, not results yet.
Snap’s quarter showed its profit improving while its advertising barely grew. Advertising revenue growth is the figure to watch when Snap reports its Q4 FY2026 results, expected in February 2027.

Maryland’s highest court heard arguments on an appeal Monday that will affect 1,300 lawsuits filed under the Child Victims Act.
The 2023 law effectively eliminated time barriers for someone to file a court claim of institutional sex abuse. At issue are the roughly 1,300 cases in which the alleged sexual assaults took place before 1982, a time when the state had absolute immunity from lawsuits. The Supreme Court of Maryland is being asked to decide if the General Assembly, when it passed the landmark 2023 law, clearly and knowingly waived that immunity.
The article is republished from Maryland Matters.
Jonathan Massey, attorney for a plaintiff known only as J.C., said the waiver of damage caps in the 2023 law are proof of the legislature’s intent.
The change “is the waiver of state sovereign immunity, and make changes that assume there will be a damages cap, assuming there will be liability to the state, right? That’s why you need a damages cap because there’s going to be liability to the state. I don’t think the legislature was silent in 2023 on the issue of sovereign immunity,” Massey said during oral arguments.
Monday’s appeal involves a claim of sexual abuse from 1977, when J.C. was a patient at the old Prince George’s Hospital Center, where she claimed a doctor molested her during a stay there.
Lawyers for the state argued that the state at the time was protected by sovereign immunity. Prior to 1982, the state could not face civil lawsuits, and the state’s lawyers asked a Prince George’s County judge to dismiss the case on those grounds.
Attorneys representing the state filed roughly 200 motions to dismiss cases involving claims before July 1, 1982. The state has argued that the legislature must expressly waive the 40-year old immunity provision, something they said the 2023 law did not do.
Judges at the Circuit Court level granted four motions at the time the appeal was filed with the state’s highest court.
The Prince George’s County court denied the state’s motion without a hearing or explanation. But judges in Frederick County and Baltimore City have agreed with the state. Each dismissed cases under the sovereign immunity argument.
The Supreme Court’s ruling on the issue comes with a dollar sign attached.
Cases involving allegations occurring before 1982 comprise about 11% of the 12,000 cases that have been filed under the Child Victims Act. The 2023 law capped damages against the state at $890,000 per occurrence, but the definition of an “occurrence” is still being debated.
The full extent of the state’s potential liability has never been publicly stated. A rough estimate shows potentially budget-busting consequences.

If lawyers for the state are successful in getting the pre-1982 cases blocked, it would reduce the state’s potential liability by “more than a billion dollars,” the Office of the Attorney General argued in a filing earlier this year.

I don’t know about you, but I have days, weeks, and months when my running is challenging.
Sometimes that challenge arises when you’re coming back from an injury or an offseason, while other times it can be due to particularly busy or stressful times in life. When that time comes, even getting out the door feels daunting. When that’s the case, a little nudge can go a long way to getting back on track.
I find that this one small promise can help me quickly return to real running: 7×7.
No fewer than four times so far this decade, I’ve gone to my tried-and-true crutch: I run seven miles a day for seven straight days. It’s a small idea, but it’s worked every time.
Every one of those times, I was in a place where even the first seven-mile run felt daunting, but I told myself I was going to do it. I got out the door, and then again the next day, and the day after that, until I’d completed seven days. If I had to walk the second half of the week, that’s fine. If I was slow as all get out, it didn’t matter. The point was to get out there and cover the ground.
After I completed that commitment, I’d gotten over that hump, that activation energy, that dark hill that stood in front of me, I found myself on a ridge I could run along. I’d renewed a habit. I could run for an hour. That was fine. If I could run for an hour every day for a week — no matter how I felt, how tired I was, or what the weather was — then I could run for an hour on any day that followed.
And while 7×7 itself was a small commitment, it actually stood in lieu of a larger one hiding behind it, and that was a recommitment to myself as a runner. It helped me re-identify as a runner and prioritize that time in my daily life.
Now, 7×7 might not be a magical commitment for you, but I bet you can find ways to jump-start your own running if you need to. Here are some thoughts on how you might do that successfully.
- Keep it short. If you’re having a rough patch in your running, it might be too much to commit to running every day for a year. But it could be five days, two weeks, every day during a vacation, or whatever timeframe works for you.
- Keep the bar low (enough). If you’re trying to overcome a hill, don’t make your challenge a mountain. While seven miles of running might seem daunting to me on the first day of 7×7, I know from decades of running that an hour is totally doable, even if it’s double what I might run during a slump. For me, even upping that to 10 miles a day might go from restarting a good habit to physically challenging.
- Make it concrete. Have numbers. If it’s going to be running a certain number of days, or if it’s a certain number of miles in a week, whatever it is, establish a concrete goal because you hit it or you don’t.

A battery storage facility sits in front of wind turbines near Palm Springs, California. States and utilities are building battery farms but many communities oppose them. (Photo by Mario Tama/Getty Images)
SNOQUALMIE, Wash. — In the race to meet the nation’s growing power demands, states and utilities are rapidly building new “battery farms” that can store energy for when customers need it most. But as the facilities grow, so too does community opposition.
The systems store banks of batteries in buildings or shipping containers. While they can take many forms, developers are increasingly building large, multi-acre projects designed to meet the needs of local utilities.
The electricity stored by such systems nationwide has grown tenfold since 2022, and it’s projected to double again by the end of 2028. State lawmakers and renewable energy advocates say battery storage is urgently needed to stabilize the grid and support the transition to clean power.

To be at the frontier of quantum computing, industry-relevant applications demand both computational quality and speed. Speed matters because a quantum computer delivers its answer in samples: each run of a quantum circuit returns one result. Scale and quality enable increasingly complex computations, but speed determines whether these demanding workloads can be completed in practical timeframes and at a reasonable cost.

In a single month, Anthropic added $10 billion to its run-rate revenue. Amendment No. 2 to its S-1, which the SEC accepted at 6:29 a.m. ET on November 10, 2026, puts the figure at about $81 billion as of October 31, 2026. The previous amendment had left that number blank.
By our calculation, the run rate was about $71 billion on September 30, which means it rose roughly 14% in one month. The expected price range is still $70 to $78 for 825,000,000 Class A shares. At the top of the range, Anthropic would raise about $64.4 billion, and the shares would be worth about $916 billion to $1.02 trillion on a basic-share count.
Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN | AMZN Price Prediction) and Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOG, NASDAQ:GOOGL) both sell Anthropic computing power and both own large stakes in it. In early afternoon trading on November 11, 2026, Amazon was down 1.32% at $267.29, and Alphabet was up 2.85% at $295.58. The filing does not explain either move.
How a 28-Day Window Becomes $81 Billion
To get run-rate revenue, Anthropic takes consumption fees from the trailing 28 days and multiplies them by 13. It then adds monthly subscription fees multiplied by 12. Because of that growth, one strong month can quickly push the reported figure up.
So the October jump is impressive, but it may not last. The filing says the figure does not replace GAAP revenue, is not a forecast, has not been independently verified, and can swing with holiday usage. It can also include amounts from customers later found violating usage policies.
Run Rate Versus Reported Revenue
GAAP revenue, the standard accounting figure, was $16.956 billion in the September quarter. That compares with $11.555 billion in the June quarter, a gain of about 46.7% by our calculation, and $1.382 billion a year earlier. Annualizing the September quarter gives about $67.8 billion (our calculation). That is below the run rate because the two numbers cover different periods.
Over the same year, customers paying $100,000 or more rose from more than 950 to more than 11,900. A wider customer base suggests revenue can hold up, but usage-linked revenue can drop as fast as it rose.
What It Means for Amazon and Alphabet
Anthropic has committed to up to 5 GW of Amazon’s Trainium chips. Amazon’s second-quarter net income included a $53.4 billion pre-tax gain, mostly from its Anthropic interest. AWS revenue rose 39% to $45.98 billion in the third quarter, although Amazon does not say how much of that came from Anthropic.
Equity stakes can also hurt reported results. Alphabet took an $8.7 billion loss on equity securities, which ended its run of EPS beats, even as Google Cloud grew 103%. Some of the money both companies invest in Anthropic comes back to them as cloud spending, so it is hard to tell how much of that cloud demand would exist without the investment.

The filing includes no forecast and no outside verification of the run rate. It does include a warning that run-rate growth will slow, possibly sharply. When winter arrives, it’s tempting to put your running goals on hold until the temperatures warm up, the days get longer, and the roads clear. Cold temperatures make it harder to leave a warm bed, while snow and ice can turn a familiar route into a much slower—and more slippery—run.
For months at a time, Michelle Baxter’s running routes in Anchorage, Alaska, were covered in packed snow and ice. After a snowstorm, plows could take days to reach every neighborhood, and by then, cars had compressed the fallen snow onto the roads. Even after the plows came through, the slick surface often remained.
Baxter—now an RRCA- and V.02-certified run coach—spent 15 years living in Alaska and training through winters like these, figuring out how to keep running through harsh, unmotivating conditions.
She trained for 12 marathons in that time, continuing to build fitness year after year. Eventually, she even achieved her most ambitious running goal: breaking three hours in the marathon. After eight years of attempting to break the barrier—and a heartbreakingly close 3:01:14 at Humpy’s Marathon in Anchorage in August 2021—Baxter finally ran a 2:58:24 at the California International Marathon in December 2021. She has since lowered her PR to 2:56:57 at the Indianapolis Monumental Marathon.
Your winter running routes may not be covered in snow and ice for six months straight, but chances are you’ll face your own challenges as the temperature drops in the coming weeks and months. The good news: Baxter’s experience can help you navigate tough terrain and make the most of your training.
Here’s how you can put her lessons to work this winter so when the ice thaws, you’re ready to run your fastest race yet.
Find Gear That Makes Winter Running Manageable
What you wear can make or break a winter run, Baxter says. When you’re too cold, too warm, or worried about taking a spill around every tight corner, it’s hard to focus on any other aspect of the run. Baxter spent years figuring out what works, and her gear advice starts with two essentials: finding reliable footwear and appropriate layers for the conditions.
→Getting a Grip on Slippery Surfaces
In Anchorage, finding reliable footing was Baxter’s biggest winter challenge. She initially resisted buying studded shoes, assuming they wouldn’t make much difference. But once she tried them, she was surprised by how much more confident she felt in every step.
For packed snow, Baxter often wore regular trainers fitted with screws in the outsoles, which she added herself.
On sheer ice, Baxter preferred shoes made with built-in carbide studs; she swears by the Icebug brand. “You can wear these shoes and make a 90-degree turn and feel so confident running on ice—like sheer ice,” Baxter says. “They were a game-changer for me.”
You may not encounter sheets of ice on your regular running routes, but consider the conditions you encounter most often and look for an option suited to them.
Now living in Minnesota, Baxter says she reaches for studded shoes if she expects at least half of a run to cover potentially snowy or icy ground. She notes that while the shoes may be slightly less comfortable than your normal trainers, protecting your body from harm is the number-one priority during the winter months of training.
“I just think it’s worth it to feel confident running on the slippery surfaces and not risk injuring yourself,” she says.
